source_text: ΛΟΓΟΣ ΚΔʹ. Εἰς τὸν ἅγιον ἱερομάρτυρα Κυπριανὸν, ἐξ ἀγροῦ μετὰ μίαν τῆς μνείας ἡμέραν ἐπανήκοντος. Αʹ. Μικροῦ Κυπριανὸς διέφυγεν ἡμᾶς· ὢ τῆς ζη μίας! καὶ ὑμεῖς ἠνέσχεσθε, οἱ πάντων μᾶλλον τὸν ἄνδρα θαυμάζοντες, καὶ ταῖς δι' ἔτους τιμῶντες ἐκεῖνον τιμαῖς τε καὶ πανηγύρεσι· Κυπριανὸς, οὗ, καὶ τοῖς τἄλλα ἐπιλήσμοσι, μεμνῆσθαι τῶν ἀναγκαίων· εἴπερ τῶν ἀρίστων μάλιστα μνημονευτέον, καὶ ὧν τὸ μεμνῆσθαι ὅσιόν τε ὁμοῦ καὶ ὠφέλιμον, Ἀλλ' ἀποδῶμεν σὺν τόκῳ τὸ χρέος, ἂν ἄρα τοσοῦτον εὐποροῦντες φανῶμεν, ἀλλὰ μὴ πάντα ὦμεν ἐνδεεῖς τε καὶ πένητες. Ἂν δὲ καὶ λίαν πένητες, οἶδ' ὅτι συγγνώσεται ἡμῖν καὶ τῆς ὑπερημερίας, καὶ τῆς πενίας, ἐπεὶ καὶ πάντα μεγαλόψυχος ὁ ἀνὴρ καὶ φιλόσοφος· μόνον ἂν, ὅτι μὴ διέφυγεν ἡμᾶς, εὐχαρι στήσωμεν. Εὐχαριστήσωμεν δέ· καὶ γὰρ ἄξιον. Ἀρκτέον δὲ οὕτως, ὡς εἰς καλὸν ὑμῖν ἐπανήκομεν, καὶ καλοῖς μέτροις Θεοῦ, τοῦ πάντα ἐν σταθμῷ καὶ μέτρῳ διορίζοντός τε καὶ διευθύνοντος, ἐκ τῆς ἡσυ χίας ἐπὶ τὸν λόγον, ἐκ τῆς φιλομάρτυρος ἐπὶ μάρτυρας, ἐκ τῆς σωματικῆς ἀνέσεως ἐπὶ τὴν πνευματικὴν ἑστίασιν. Βʹ. Ἐποθοῦμεν ὑμᾶς, ὦ τέκνα, καὶ ἀντεποθούμε θα τοῖς ἴσοις μέτροις· πείθομαι γάρ. Ὁρᾶτε πατρὸς εὐγνωμοσύνην· καὶ τὸ ἐμαυτοῦ λέγω, καὶ τὸ ὑμέτερον μαρτυρῶ, καὶ τοσοῦτον διαζευχθέντες ἀλλή λων, ὅσον τὸν πόθον γνωρίσαι καὶ δοκιμάσαι τῇ ἀπο στάσει, καθάπερ οἱ ζωγράφοι τοὺς πίνακας, πάλιν συνήλθομεν. Ὡς μέγα μνήμης ἐμπύρευμα, καὶ βραχεῖα συνήθεια φίλων, τοῖς τε ἀγαπητικοῖς τὸν τρόπον, καὶ Θεοῦ μιμουμένοις φιλανθρωπίαν! Πῶς δὲ οὐκ ἐμέλλομεν, οἱ Χριστοῦ μαθηταὶ, τοῦ κενωθέντος δι' ἡμᾶς μέχρι δούλου μορφῆς, καὶ ξένους ὄντας τῶν οὐρανίων πρὸς ἑαυτὸν συναγαγόντος, ἀνθ έξεσθαί τε καὶ περιέξεσθαι ἀλλήλων, καὶ τηρήσειν τὴν ἑνότητα τοῦ πνεύματος ἐν τῷ συνδεσμῷ τῆς εἰρήνης, ἣ νόμου καὶ προφητῶν ἐστι μυστήριον, εἴτ' οὖν κεφάλαιον; Γʹ. Ἓν μὲν δὴ τοῦτο τῆς εὐεργεσίας καὶ πρῶτον, τὸ ὡς τάχιστα προσδραμεῖν ἀλλήλοις καὶ περιπτύξα σθαι. Οὐδὲ γὰρ φέρει τὴν ἀναβολὴν ὁ ζῆλος· καὶ βίος ὅλος ἡμέρα μία τοῖς πόθῳ κάμνουσιν. Δεύτερον δὲ, ὃ καὶ μέγιστον, τὸ μὴ κατόπιν ἑορτῆς δραμεῖν, μηδὲ μαρτύρων μυσταγωγίας ἀπολειφθῆναι, καὶ τῆς ἐντεῦθεν ἐγγινομένης ἡμῖν τρυφῆς τε καὶ ἀναψύξεως. Ἐγὼ γὰρ τἄλλα μὲν ὁμολογῶ παντὸς εἶναι νωθέστερος· καὶ πάντα πόθον ἀπεσεισάμην, ἀφ' οὗ Χριστῷ συνεταξάμην, καὶ οὐδὲν αἱρεῖμε τῶν ὅσα τερπνὰ τοῖς ἄλλοις καὶ περισπούδαστα· οὐ πλοῦτος ὁ κάτω συρόμενος καὶ περιτρεπόμενος, οὐ γαστρὸς ἡδοναὶ, καὶ κόρος πατὴρ ὕβρεως, οὐκ ἐσθὴς μαλακή τε καὶ περιῤῥέουσα, οὐ λίθων διαύγειαι καὶ χάριτες, οὐκ ἀκοὴ γοητεύουσα, οὐκ ὄσφρησις ἐκθηλύνουσα, οὐ κρότοι δήμων καὶ θεάτρων ἐκμαίνοντες, ὧν πάλαι τοῖς βουλομένοις παρεχωρήσαμεν· οὐχ ὅσα τῆς πρώτης γεύσεως ἡμῶν, ἐξ ἧς ἀπολώλαμεν, ἔκγονα· ἀλλὰ καὶ πολλὴν εὐήθειαν καταγινώσκω τῶν κρατεῖσθαι τούτοις ἀνεχομένων, καὶ τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς εὐγενὲς δια φθείρειν τῇ περὶ ταῦτα μικροπρεπείᾳ, καὶ ὡς ἑστῶσι προστιθεμένων τοῖς φεύγουσιν. Ἐκείνου δὲ λίαν ἀπλήστως ἔχω καὶ περιέχομαι, καὶ τοῦ πάθους ἐμαυ τὸν ἀποδέχομαι· μαρτύρων τιμαῖς ἐπιτέρπομαι, καὶ ἀθλητῶν αἵμασιν ἐπαγάλλομαι· καὶ ἄλλων μὲν οἱ ἆθλοι καὶ τὸ κρατεῖν, ἐμοὶ δὲ οἱ στέφανοι.
thought_title: Gregory's return and the bond of love
orientation: Gregory of Nazianzus is opening his panegyric for the hieromartyr Cyprian, explaining that he has just returned from the countryside one day after the annual commemoration and is now addressing the congregation.
pass_a_gloss: Oration 24. On the holy hieromartyr Cyprian, when he returned from the countryside one day after the commemoration. 1. Cyprian almost escaped us; oh the loss! And you endured it, you who admire the man more than all, and honor him with yearly honors and festivals; Cyprian, of whom, even for those forgetful of other things, it is necessary to remember the essential things; if indeed of the best men especially one must remember, and of those whose remembrance is both holy and beneficial. But let us pay back the debt with interest, if indeed we appear to have such resources, and not be entirely lacking and poor. But if we are also very poor, I know that he will forgive us both for the delay and for the poverty, since the man is also entirely great-souled and a philosopher; only if we give thanks that he did not escape us. And let us give thanks; for it is fitting. And we must begin thus, that we have returned to you for good, and by good measures of God, who determines and directs all things in weight and measure, from stillness to speech, from the martyr-loving one to martyrs, from bodily rest to spiritual feasting. 2. We longed for you, O children, and we were longed for in return with equal measures; for I am persuaded. You see a father's gratitude; and I say what is mine, and I bear witness to what is yours, and having been separated from each other just so much as to recognize and test the longing by the absence, just as painters do with their panels, we have come together again. How great is the fire of memory, and brief is the companionship of friends, for those who are loving in character and who imitate God's love for humanity! And how were we not going to, we disciples of Christ, who emptied himself for us even to the form of a slave, and gathered to himself those who were strangers to heavenly things, to hold fast to one another and cling to one another, and to keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace, which is the mystery, or rather the sum, of the law and the prophets? 3. This then is one benefit and the first, that we ran to one another as quickly as possible and embraced. For zeal does not bear delay; and a whole life is one day for those who are weary with longing. And the second, which is also the greatest, is not to run behind the feast, nor to be left behind from the initiation into the martyrs, and from the delight and refreshment that comes to us from this. For I confess that in other things I am more sluggish than everyone; and I have shaken off every longing, since I enlisted with Christ, and I choose none of the things that are pleasant to others and eagerly sought after; not wealth that is dragged along the ground and overturned, not pleasures of the belly, and satiety the father of insolence, not soft and flowing clothing, not the brilliance and graces of stones, not hearing that bewitches, not smell that makes effeminate, not the applause of peoples and theaters that drives mad, which we long ago yielded to those who want them; not all the offspring of our first taste, from which we have perished; but I also condemn the great foolishness of those who allow themselves to be ruled by these things, and to corrupt the nobility of the soul by the pettiness about these things, and who attach themselves to things that are fleeing as if they were standing. But of that I am exceedingly insatiable and I cling to it, and I approve of my own passion; I delight in the honors of martyrs, and I exult in the blood of athletes; and for others belong the contests and the victory, but for me the crowns.

choices.why: The glossary specifies hieromartyr as the rendering for a martyr who was also a bishop or priest, and Cyprian was a bishop.
The glossary specifies martyr as the rendering for μάρτυς, one who has borne witness to Christ by suffering or death.
The glossary specifies athlete as the rendering for ἀθλητής, one who contends in the martyr's contest.
The glossary specifies crown as the rendering for στέφανος, the crown of victory awarded to martyrs.
The glossary specifies philosophy as the Christian way of life, and here the adjective describes Cyprian's character as one who lives that way.
The term refers to the sacred celebration or initiation connected with the martyrs' commemoration; rendering it as initiation preserves the cultic sense.

pass_b_english: Oration 24. On the holy hieromartyr Cyprian, on the speaker's return from the country one day after the commemoration. Cyprian almost slipped away from us—what a loss! And you allowed it, you who admire the man more than anyone and honor him year after year with feasts and public celebrations. Cyprian—the one whom even those who forget everything else must remember among the things that matter, if indeed the best are most to be remembered, and those whose memory is at once holy and profitable.

But let us pay the debt with interest, if we can show ourselves to have such resources—if indeed we are not altogether lacking and poor. And if we are very poor, I know he will forgive us both the delay and the poverty, since the man is in every way great-souled and a philosopher. Only let us give thanks that he did not escape us. Let us give thanks, for it is right.

We must begin this way: we have returned to you at a good moment, by God's good measures—God who orders and directs all things in weight and measure—from stillness to speech, from love of the martyr to the martyrs, from bodily rest to spiritual feasting.

We were longing for you, my children, and you were longing for us in equal measure—I am convinced of it. You see a father's right feeling: I speak of my own, and I testify to yours. We were separated from one another just long enough to recognize and test our longing through absence, as painters do with their panels, and now we have come together again.

How great a spark of memory even a brief companionship of friends is—for those whose character is loving and who imitate God's love for humanity! How could we not, as disciples of Christ, who emptied himself for us to the point of taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and gathered us, strangers to the heavenly things, to himself—how could we not hold fast to one another and cling to one another, and keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3), which is the mystery, or rather the sum, of the law and the prophets?

This, then, is the first and foremost benefit: that we ran to one another as quickly as possible and embraced. For zeal does not tolerate delay, and a whole lifetime is a single day to those worn out with longing.

The second benefit, and the greatest, is that we did not come running after the feast was over, nor were we left behind from the initiation into the martyrs and the delight and refreshment that comes to us from it.

For I confess that in everything else I am more sluggish than anyone. I have shaken off every desire since I enlisted with Christ, and I choose none of the things that others find delightful and eagerly pursue: not wealth that is dragged along the ground and overturned, not the pleasures of the belly and the satiety that is the father of insolence, not soft flowing clothing, not the brilliance and charms of precious stones, not music that bewitches the ear, not fragrance that makes one effeminate, not the applause of crowds and theaters that drives men mad—all of which we long ago surrendered to those who want them—not any of the offspring of that first taste of ours, through which we were ruined. Indeed, I condemn the great foolishness of those who allow themselves to be mastered by these things, corrupting the nobility of the soul with pettiness about them, and clinging to things that are passing as if they were permanent.

But for that other thing I have an insatiable hunger and I cling to it, and I approve of this passion in myself. I delight in the honors of the martyrs, and I rejoice in the blood of the athletes. Others have the contests and the victory; mine are the crowns.

problems.quote: unless we prove utterly lacking and poor
problems.source_quote: ἀλλὰ μὴ πάντα ὦμεν ἐνδεεῖς τε καὶ πένητες
problems.why: Source says 'lest we be' (negative purpose), not 'unless'. The fear is of total destitution, not a conditional exception.
problems.fix: if indeed we are not altogether lacking and poor
problems.ruling: ἀλλὰ μὴ...ὦμεν is negative purpose ('lest we be'), not conditional 'unless we prove'—changes grammatical force and rhetorical effect.

edits.old: unless we prove utterly lacking and poor
edits.new: if indeed we are not altogether lacking and poor

fixed: Changed 'unless we prove utterly lacking and poor' to 'if indeed we are not altogether lacking and poor' because the source ἀλλὰ μὴ πάντα ὦμεν ἐνδεεῖς τε καὶ πένητες expresses a negative purpose ('lest we be'), not a conditional exception.

problems.source_quote: Ὡς μέγα μνήμης ἐμπύρευμα, καὶ βραχεῖα συνήθεια φίλων

problems.fix: How great a spark of memory even a brief companionship of friends is

problems.quote: On the holy hieromartyr Cyprian, on his return from the country one day after the commemoration.
problems.source_quote: Εἰς τὸν ἅγιον ἱερομάρτυρα Κυπριανὸν, ἐξ ἀγροῦ μετὰ μίαν τῆς μνείας ἡμέραν ἐπανήκοντος.
problems.why: The genitive absolute is the speaker returning a day late, not Cyprian returning.
problems.fix: On the holy hieromartyr Cyprian, delivered on the speaker’s return from the country one day after the commemoration.
problems.ruling: ἐπανήκοντος agrees with Κυπριανὸν in the accusative-looking heading, but the speaker returns ('ἐπανήκομεν', 'ὡς εἰς καλὸν ὑμῖν ἐπανήκομεν'); the English says Cyprian returns, which misleads.

last_rejected.quote: as painters do with their panels
last_rejected.why: Source says painters test panels by stepping back; English omits the testing purpose of the comparison.
last_rejected.fix: as painters step back from their panels to test them
last_rejected.ruling: καθάπερ οἱ ζωγράφοι τοὺς πίνακας: 'as painters do with their panels' captures the comparison; testing purpose is interpretive inference, not required.

last_rejected.quote: and clinging to things that are passing as if they were permanent
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἑστῶσι προστιθεμένων τοῖς φεύγουσιν
last_rejected.why: Source says 'adding to fleeing things as if they were standing'—i.e., treating transient things as permanent, but English reverses the metaphor's direction.
last_rejected.fix: and adding to fleeting things as if they were permanent
last_rejected.ruling: ὡς ἑστῶσι προστιθεμένων τοῖς φεύγουσιν: 'clinging to things passing as permanent' correctly renders the sense; metaphor direction preserved in meaning.

last_rejected.why: ἠνέσχεσθε means 'you bore/endured it', not 'you allowed it'; sense is 'you too endured this loss'
last_rejected.fix: and you endured it as well
last_rejected.ruling: ἠνέσχεσθε from ἀνέχω commonly means 'endured/bore'; 'allowed it' is a reasonable rendering of bearing the loss without protest.

last_rejected.quote: I am more sluggish than anyone
last_rejected.why: νωθέστερος means 'slower/more dull' but context shows Gregory means he is slower to pursue worldly things, not absolutely 'more sluggish than anyone'
last_rejected.fix: I confess that in all else I am slower than anyone
last_rejected.ruling: παντὸς νωθέστερος 'more sluggish than anyone' fits; context clarifies scope. Not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: Others have the contests and the victory; mine are the crowns
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ ἄλλων μὲν οἱ ἆθλοι καὶ τὸ κρατεῖν, ἐμοὶ δὲ οἱ στέφανοι
last_rejected.why: κρατεῖν means 'to prevail/to win', but the contrast is between others' active struggles and Gregory's contemplative enjoyment of the results; 'victory' slightly flattens the paradox
last_rejected.fix: For others the contests and the winning; for me the crowns
last_rejected.ruling: κρατεῖν 'to prevail/win' = 'victory'; contrast preserved. Mere preference, not error.
